meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'hello'.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to give; (imperative) let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'hello', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello, Pavel. What do you want?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how; as', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'matter; thing to do' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Borrowed via Polish/German from Greek 'problema' (something thrown forward, a task or question).

examples.trans: I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'my, mine', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?
Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).

examples.trans: And the kitchen is over there.
We are sitting in the kitchen.

examples.text: Проходите, пожалуйста! Как видите, большой коридор, а там кухня.
examples.trans: Come on in, please! As you can see, a big hall, and the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'иний'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('blue, dark blue').

examples.trans: Did you find that little blue bottle?
Did you find the vial? That little blue bottle.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'time' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'порить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to argue, to dispute', paired with 'поспорить'.

examples.trans: That's a nightmare, I don't argue.

examples.text: Это кошмар, я не спорю. Но зачем на видео снимать?
examples.trans: That's a nightmare, I don't argue. But why film it on video?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'work, job' in everyday Russian.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тоить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cost; to be worth'.

examples.trans: And how much does the console cost?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

посадить.gloss: to seat; to plant; to put in prison

meanings.en: to seat; to plant; to put in prison
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'садить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to seat; to plant; to put in prison', paired with 'сажать'.

examples.text: Аникеев? Ну что, проворовался? Да я тебя посажу!
examples.trans: Anikeev? Well then, caught stealing? I'll put you in prison!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'they', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common masculine noun meaning 'fridge' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The milk is in the fridge.

examples.text: Курица? Нет. А чей это холодильник?
examples.trans: Chicken? No. And whose fridge is this?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'then, back then', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

включить.gloss: to turn on, to plug in

meanings.en: to turn on, to plug in
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to turn on, to plug in', paired with 'включать'.

examples.trans: I'll plug it in right now.

examples.text: Сейчас включу. Он у нас быстро всё вспомнит.
examples.trans: I'll plug it in right now. He'll remember everything quickly with us.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'brain' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There are brains, but no money.

examples.text: В Москве вам дают деньги на дорогую одежду, а мозги не дают.
examples.trans: In Moscow they give you money for expensive clothes, but they don't give you brains.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'ставить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to force, make', paired with 'заставлять'.

examples.text: Я своё мнение не менял. Это меня коллектив заставил.
examples.trans: I haven't changed my opinion. The staff forced me into this.

examples.text: Я хотел их заставить выучить стихотворение Блока!
examples.trans: I wanted to make them memorise a poem by Blok!

examples.text: Он заставил выключить свет даже в зале.
examples.trans: He forced the light to be turned off even in the dining hall.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'ступить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'yield / give in'.

examples.text: Он в нужный момент находит силу уступить.
examples.trans: At the right moment he finds the strength to yield.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и уступить вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and yield on time.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

examples.text: Это Паша, мой заместитель. Это Ваня, друг моего детства.
examples.trans: This is Pasha, my deputy. This is Vanya, my childhood friend.
